link.page: What serve and return actually means

music.brief: Sparse felt piano, slow, room tone, no melody that resolves, 30 seconds.

labels.title: The drop
labels.text: A spoon goes over the edge for the ninth time. Not an accident, and not a test of you. At this age, letting go on purpose is new, and a thing that disappears and lands with a sound is worth repeating.

labels.title: Her eyes go to you
labels.text: Watch where she looks the moment it lands. Usually at your face. The drop is only half of the game. The other half is what you do next, and she is waiting for it.

labels.title: A serve
labels.text: Any bid for your attention counts as a serve: a look, a sound, a point, a spoon on the floor. Returning it, with a word or a face or the spoon, is the ordinary exchange that builds attention and language.

labels.title: Your return
labels.text: "Spoon. Down it goes." A name for the thing and the event, then a pause so she can answer. The return does not have to be fun or patient every time. It has to happen more often than not.

labels.title: A conceptual reading
labels.text: What is drawn here is what may be developing in a baby of this age in general. It is not what this child is thinking, and it is not a measure of anything.

slides.head: What to try at the table
items: Name it once, plainly: "spoon, down." Then wait a beat.
Return the look before the spoon. Her face is the serve.
Three rounds is plenty. Then the spoon stays on the tray.
On tired days, a glance and a word is a full return.

sources: Center on the Developing Child, Harvard University. Serve and return. developingchild.harvard.edu/science/key-concepts/serve-and-return
